map.concept.config.title: Configuration
map.concept.config.body:
A setting the agent's author made adjustable without touching the prompt.

Take the "Weekly report" agent. The Slack channel it posts to never changes from one week to the next, but it does change from one company to the next: that is configuration, set once at install time. The week to analyse changes at every launch: that is input.

Same shape in the manifest, two lifetimes. Hence this card's place, next to the model rather than on the agent's axis: configuration and model are both settings of your installation, not data flowing through the agent.

Two things are editable here. The header pencil changes which settings the agent DECLARES, which touches its manifest. Clicking a row sets its VALUE for this application: the same definition installed twice can post to two different channels.
map.concept.schedules.title: Schedules
map.concept.schedules.body:
A schedule fires the agent on its own, at a fixed time, with nobody clicking. Think of an alarm clock set on the agent: every Monday at 8am, off it goes.

An agent can have several, or none and only ever run by hand. A schedule can pin a specific version of the agent: when it does, it runs a different definition than the one drawn here, and the card says so.
map.concept.input.title: Input
map.concept.input.body:
What a caller must hand the agent when starting it. It is a form described in the manifest: every field has a name, a type, and may be required.

An agent with no input starts without asking for anything. An agent with one refuses to start when a required field is missing, whether the call comes from the UI, a schedule or the API.
map.concept.agent.title: Agent
map.concept.agent.body:
An agent is first a prompt: plain-language instructions describing its job. Everything else on this map exists to serve that text, giving it a model to think with, tools to act with, and a contract for handing back its result.

The timeout shown is the limit past which a run is cut off.
map.concept.model.title: Model
map.concept.model.body:
The language model the agent thinks with. It is not part of the manifest: it is an organization setting, so the same agent can run on a different model from one installation to the next.

With nothing chosen for this agent, it inherits the organization default. With no model available at all, it cannot run.
map.concept.output.title: Output
map.concept.output.body:
The shape the result must take. Declaring an output moves the agent from free-form prose to data another program can consume.

Not to be confused with the "Structured output" system tool: that tool is how the agent emits its result, while this card describes the expected shape. Declaring an output is in fact what makes that tool mandatory.
map.concept.toolbox.title: Integrations
map.concept.toolbox.body:
An integration is an outside service the agent can call: Gmail, Slack, ClickUp. It brings two inseparable things, the tools (what can be done) and the credentials (the right to do it).

It is the agent's only way out. Credentials are never handed to it: they are injected separately, at call time, by a component it does not control.

Declaring an integration is not enough to make it usable: it must also be enabled in the application, and a connection must exist.
map.concept.skills.title: Skills
map.concept.skills.body:
A skill is a method sheet the agent reads when it needs it: a procedure to follow, a format to respect, a piece of domain know-how. It is text, not code, and it grants access to nothing.

The difference from the prompt is timing: the prompt is present on every run, a skill is loaded only when relevant. So you can accumulate many without weighing down each run.
map.concept.mcpServers.title: MCP servers
map.concept.mcpServers.body:
MCP is the standard protocol through which an agent discovers and calls tools. An MCP server is a tool provider plugged straight into the agent.

The difference from an integration: an integration adds credential and permission handling on top. An MCP server declared here is used as is.
map.concept.systemTools.title: System tools
map.concept.systemTools.body:
Tools provided by the platform itself, with no outside service involved: returning a result, writing to the log, keeping a note from one run to the next, publishing a document.

Most must be granted explicitly in the manifest, one by one. Two escape that rule and are always there: reading back the memory archive, and the history of past runs. Reading what the agent itself produced carries no risk, whereas writing to memory or publishing a document does.

integrationEditor.auths.empty: No auth declared. Add at least one.
integrationEditor.auths.apiCallDesc: Gives the agent a generic api_call tool that injects this auth's credentials into HTTP calls. Independent of the MCP source.

integrationEditor.auths.defaultScopesReq: Wildcard tools enabled: declare non-empty default_scopes here, or add a non-OAuth2 auth method (api_key/basic/custom/mtls).
integrationEditor.auths.credentialFields: Expected field names (e.g. api_key). Each becomes a required string property.
integrationEditor.toolsPolicy.title: Tools policy
integrationEditor.toolsPolicy.help: Per-MCP-tool metadata — the OAuth scopes each tool requires, per auth method.
integrationEditor.allowUndeclaredTools.d: Lets an agent opt into every upstream MCP tool via tools: "*". Under OAuth2, the agent's scopes fall back to the selected auth's default_scopes. Non-OAuth2 auths (api_key, basic, custom, mtls) are wildcard-usable by default (no scope mechanism). Enable only when the server's tool surface grows faster than manifest republishes.
integrationEditor.allowUndeclaredTools.r: Requires at least one wildcard-usable auth: non-OAuth2 (api_key/basic/custom/mtls) or OAuth2 with non-empty default_scopes.
integrationEditor.toolsPolicy.requiredSc: Scopes this tool needs, per auth method. Only the auth used at runtime requests them — another auth (e.g. a PAT) can still serve the tool.
integrationEditor.toolsPolicy.noAuths: Declare an auth method first to assign scopes.
